item.title: Xi to attend BRICS summit in New Delhi
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-11
Xi to attend BRICS summit in New Delhi Meeting expected to boost cooperation, amplify voice of Global South, say experts President Xi Jinping will attend the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi from Saturday to Sunday at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Foreign Ministry spokesperson announced on Thursday. The meeting is widely expected to inject fresh momentum into BRICS cooperation, help BRICS countries and the wider Global South expand the pie of win-win cooperation, and reaffirm their commitment to multilateralism, experts said. India has adopted "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" as the theme of its 2026 BRICS presidency, with a stated emphasis on a people-centric approach and stronger cooperation among countries of the Global South. Initially comprising Brazil, Russia, India and China, the grouping later welcomed South Africa and has since expanded further to 11 members. According to figures published on India's official BRICS presidency website, the 11 members account for about 49.5 percent of the world's population, 40 percent of global GDP and 26 percent of global trade. "Xi's attendance once again demonstrates the importance that China consistently attaches to BRICS cooperation, the development of the mechanism and the common development of Global South countries," said Su Xiaohui, an associate research fellow at the China Institute of International Studies. China's role in advancing BRICS cooperation will again be highlighted at the summit, she said. Cooperation with other BRICS countries has long been a priority of China's foreign policy. Xi's first appearance at a major international multilateral meeting after becoming Chinese president was at the fifth BRICS Summit, held in Durban, South Africa, in March 2013. Wang Youming, a researcher on developing countries at the China Institute of International Studies, said the upcoming summit holds particular significance, as it coincides with the 20th anniversary of the launch of BRICS cooperation. "One of the biggest highlights will be Xi's trip to India after seven years," Wang said. "China and India are not only close neighbors, but also founding members and major participants in BRICS. The state of their relationship has a direct bearing on the development of the mechanism." China and India have expressed mutual support for each other in hosting BRICS events, with India holding the rotating presidency this year and China set to assume the presidency next year. "Multilateral platforms can create opportunities for bilateral engagement, while improving bilateral relations can in turn facilitate coordination within multilateral mechanisms," Wang said. At a time when unilateral trade measures and disruptions to global industrial and supply chains are placing mounting pressure on developing economies, the summit is expected to amplify the voice of the Global South and strengthen coordination in upholding an open world economy and the multilateral trading system, he added. Wang said BRICS cooperation had gradually moved beyond broad policy declarations toward concrete programs involving small and medium-sized enterprises, cities, young people and people-to-people exchanges. According to Wang, emerging sectors such as the digital economy, green development and artificial intelligence are also likely to provide new areas of growth for BRICS cooperation. Emmanuel Frimpong Sarpong, who holds a PhD from the University of Nottingham Ningbo China and is the lead author of a study on China's role in BRICS, said China has played an instrumental role in the development of the BRICS mechanism. He described the New Development Bank as one of the grouping's most significant achievements. By the end of 2025, the bank had approved $42.9 billion in financing for 139 projects covering clean energy, transportation, water and sanitation, environmental protection, and social and digital infrastructure, according to the bank. mojingxi@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: China shakes, stirs Asia's best bars list
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-11
At Asia's 50 Best Bars awards ceremony in Macao this summer, the spotlight finally fell on an establishment tucked behind a traditional Cantonese storefront in Guangzhou's historic Dongshankou neighborhood. Hope & Sesame was named Asia's No 1 bar — the first time a venue on the Chinese mainland has taken top spot. "When they announced the No 3 bar, that feeling was already like being No 1 … So when they actually call you, it's very crazy," said Bastien Ciocca, one of the bar's co-founders. More significantly, it was not an isolated victory. The 2026 list featured seven bars from the Chinese mainland, with Hope & Sesame, MO Bar Shenzhen and Obsidian Bar, all in Guangdong province, ranked in the top 10. Other mainland entries that made the list were Pony Up in Shanghai, CMYK in Changsha, Hunan province, Ralph's Bar in Chengdu, Sichuan province, and Tiao in Beijing. The results represent the culmination of the local industry's development, with several mainland bars repeatedly recognized in recent years. Together, they point to broader growth. China's bar scene is expanding beyond Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangdong's Guangzhou and Shenzhen into regional cities, developing distinctive local expressions and boosting exchanges with the global industry. Beyond major cities Liu Ming, co-founder of CMYK, has worked in the bar industry for 27 years and divides the development of the cocktail scene into three stages. "The domestic cocktail industry has changed dramatically since I returned to China in 2012," he said. From 2012 to 2016, cocktail culture was concentrated mainly in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Chengdu, with foreign bartenders arriving to open venues and Chinese bartenders returning from overseas. Between 2016 and the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, cocktail bars spread to more cities, while Beijing and Shanghai developed increasingly international scenes. Liu said at that time there were at least 40 cocktail bars within walking distance of one another around Beijing's Sanlitun area, with more than 20 offering high-quality drinks. The post-pandemic period brought a third stage: rapid growth across the country, accompanied by a high closure rate of establishments. "The barriers to entry are too low," Liu said. "Many people lack experience in service, menu design and cost accounting, and they simply cannot make the numbers work." The geographical spread of the industry, however, is clearly changing. "When Asia's 50 Best Bars launched back in 2016, we noticed that all of the ranked bars were in what you'd consider 'cocktail capital cities'. Now, we're seeing real diversification," said Emma Sleight, head of content for Asia's 50 Best Bars. CMYK's continued presence on the list demonstrates that regional cities can build sustainable cocktail ecosystems, while destinations such as Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, are also beginning to attract international attention. The rankings also entice visitors to discover cities through their bar scenes. For regional venues, however, survival depends heavily on local tourism and foot traffic. Liu calculates that a 30-seat bar aiming to fill its seats every day needs roughly 210 to 300 customers a week. Relying entirely on regulars for survival is difficult. "For a large bar, you need regular customers to provide a safety net and tourists to add value," he said. He also believes bars need to form clusters. "The bar industry is an ecosystem. One bar dominating on its own simply doesn't work." Ralph's Bar in Chengdu represents another business model, bringing together the local expertise of Hope& Sesame and the resources and identity of luxury brand Ralph Lauren. "We see the fusion not as a simple mix of East and West, but as a dialogue between Ralph Lauren's American sensibility and the cultural energy of Chengdu," a Ralph Lauren spokesperson told China Daily. The spokesperson added: "The city's rich food and tea culture also sharpens our focus on texture, aroma and balance. Chengdu guests have exceptionally refined palates, so every ingredient must have a purpose."

item.title: China, US call for deeper health cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-11
China, US call for deeper health cooperation Chinese and US officials and health experts have called for deeper health cooperation between the two countries, saying that medicine and public health can serve as a durable platform to advance the shared goal of promoting human wellness. Vice-Foreign Minister Ma Zhaoxu said that for more than half a century, China and the United States have cooperated on a wide range of health-related topics, including health policy, emerging and known infectious diseases, chronic disease prevention and treatment, medical research and clinical care technology. The two countries also worked closely to fight the Ebola outbreak and address global health challenges together, Ma said on Thursday during an event marking the 105th anniversary of Peking Union Medical College Hospital in Beijing. The event saw Chinese and US officials, medical scientists and workers pay tribute to the two countries' health exchanges through history. "Health cooperation between China and the US has generated fruitful outcomes thanks to mutual efforts," Ma said. He added that with the emergence of new global health challenges, China and the US are expected to further strengthen health dialogues and medical education exchanges, encourage visits among physicians, scholars and students, and deepen cooperation in areas such as infectious disease response and cancer management. Peking Union Medical College Hospital, or PUMCH, was founded by the US-based Rockefeller Foundation through its division, the China Medical Board, in 1921 and is one of the most prestigious hospitals in China. Zhang Shuyang, president of PUMCH, said that the hospital's development is closely intertwined with the US medical, health and science sector. A number of US medical experts who practiced and taught at the hospital contributed to its growth through their outstanding work, while their experiences here also became a highlight of their careers, she said. She cited Oswald Hope Robertson, an English-born US medical scientist who established the world's first blood bank during World War I, as an example. Robertson worked at the hospital as its second director of internal medicine, established pneumonia as a research focus and continued to pursue the field with dedication after returning to the US. She added that after the establishment of China-US diplomatic relations in the 1970s, the first nongovernmental academic group to visit the US from China was a medical delegation. "Today, the hospital maintains regular communication with more than 20 leading medical institutions or large companies in the US, recording over 300 mutual visits annually," she said. Zhang stressed that the hospital welcomes US experts, scholars and young people to visit and connect with Chinese medical workers, and will strengthen efforts to advance clinical collaboration and the translation of joint research results. At Thursday's event, PUMCH and the China Medical Board signed a third five-year cooperation memorandum. Roger Glass, president of the China Medical Board, said the hospital's development is a living testament to the enduring value of people-to-people friendship and academic exchanges between the two countries. He said the partnership between the two institutions is founded on shared commitments, scientific rigor, professional excellence, service to society and investment in the future generation of health and medicine. "Through further partnerships, we aim to support the hospital's continued growth and to establish a mechanism for academic exchange between the US and China," Glass said. He added that the renewed partnership comes at a time when sustained and constructive communication between the US and China is especially important. "Medicine, health and education provide a uniquely durable platform for dialogue and cooperation," he said. As collaboration brings together educators, researchers and institutional leaders from both countries "through a shared professional language and a common evidence-based approach to problem solving", Glass expressed hope for accelerating the development of disease prevention strategies and cures, and extending healthy longevity together. David Perdue, US ambassador to China, said the two countries have an opportunity to collaborate on shared health challenges including the rising burden of chronic disease and care for aging populations. He said the development of PUMCH is a shining example of what can be achieved when China and the US cooperate and strive together for the goal of improving healthcare in the world. Perdue noted that China has emerged as a competitor in biological and pharmaceutical innovation, a field where the US has long been in a world-leading position. However, competition and cooperation are never mutually exclusive. wangxiaoyu@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: A picture paints a thousand words
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-11
A single image can bridge centuries and continents. That vision came to life on Saturday at Photo Beijing 2026, where photographers, artists, scholars, and industry professionals from China and abroad gathered at the China Millennium Monument in Beijing, not simply to display photographs, but to spark conversations about where the medium has been and where it is heading. The annual event is jointly organized by the China Artistic Photography Society, the China Photographers Association, the China News Photography Society and Capital Culture Technology Group. This year's theme, "The Image: Resonance, Insight", explores the dual role of photography in the age of artificial intelligence: as a medium for emotional resonance and as a critical lens for examining machine-driven visual transformation. In his keynote address, Yang Yuanxing, founder of the event and chairman of the organizing committee, said this year's edition focuses on the theme of "Resonance and Insight". "Resonance" refers to the ability of photography to connect individual experience with public emotion, allowing visual media to generate social resonance and foster a sense of collective identity. "Insight", meanwhile, calls for closer examination of visual transformation in the age of AI, raising critical questions about photographic authenticity, authorship, and public responsibility. "The goal is to use the power of images to build consensus while safeguarding the value of photography amid technological shifts, and to explore innovative pathways for Chinese visual culture to engage with the world," he says. Organized around this theme, this year's event comprises five major clusters: contemporary narratives, photographic history, heritage continuity, artistic practice, and industry ecosystem. More than 20 exhibitions, symposiums and other activities are being held through Sunday. Among the notable exhibitions, Through the Lens of Photographic History — Classic Works from the Collection of the Hungarian Museum of Photography showcases more than 100 high-quality reproductions from the Hungarian museum, most of which are being shown in China for the first time. Hungary occupies a unique place in the history of world photography and has nurtured many pioneering photographers who helped shape the art form in the 20th century. The exhibition uses a selection of landmark works to trace the development of Hungarian photography, says Zhao Yingxin, the Chinese curator of the display. Through these works, visitors can see how the visual language of modern photography emerged, broke new ground, and continued to evolve. The exhibition, therefore, provides a rare point of reference for the study of global photographic history in China, Zhao adds. "Photography is a universal language that needs no translation. A single photograph transcends geography and language, enabling mutual observation and dialogue between different civilizations," said Peter Baki, director of the Hungarian Museum of Photography, at the opening ceremony of the exhibition on Saturday. "The exhibition not only reviews the history of Hungarian photography, but also represents a cultural dialogue between China and Hungary bonded by the power of imagery," he added. Another highlight is a photographic exhibition devoted to ancient Chinese architecture, featuring works by participants of all ages from 31 provinces, autonomous regions and municipalities. The photographs span palaces, temples, and rural dwellings, capturing everything from sweeping panoramic views to intricate architectural details, and from buildings in their natural surroundings to the efforts to protect and restore them. "We hope that through these images, more people can come to see both the form and spirit of ancient Chinese architecture, appreciate its craftsmanship and construction wisdom, and feel the history and emotional memories embedded within. Together, we invite people to cherish and safeguard the precious cultural heritage," says Su Tangshi, curator of the exhibition. Initiated in 2013, the annual event has grown into a professional and influential cultural platform. To date, it has hosted more than 530 thematic exhibitions and over 260 academic dialogues, bringing together photographers and institutions from nearly 100 countries and regions worldwide.

item.title: Visitors discover an oasis of relaxation in the Kubuqi desert
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-11
In late July, Yu Xiaohui drove hundreds of kilometers from Beijing to the eastern tip of the Kubuqi Desert in Ordos, Inner Mongolia autonomous region, because her 9-year-old daughter wanted to see sand. She expected a barren wasteland. Instead, she found a desert playground of luxury hotels, water parks, cable cars and camel rides. "It's not exactly what I pictured," she said. "It feels like people and nature are really connected here." Once one of China's most inhospitable landscapes, the Kubuqi Desert has seen its outer edges transformed into a sprawling resort complex. The desertification control rate has climbed from 4.6 percent at the turn of the century to some 50 percent today — a turnaround that authorities said marks a historic shift from losing the battle against the encroaching desert to winning it. An example of that change is Xiangshawan, or "singing sand bay" — a 5A-level scenic area, China's highest tourism rating — named for the low hum that its dunes emit when wind passes over them. The sound comes from honeycomb-like pores in the sand grains that vibrate under pressure. Opened for day visitors in 1984 as a simple tourist attraction, it evolved into a full-fledged resort complex after its 1999 corporate restructuring, earning its name as the nation's first desert resort. Visitors can enter by cable car, then travel between resort islands on vintage trains or off-road vehicles. Camels also carry tourists across the dunes. The resort's centerpiece is the Lotus Hotel, a white, flower-shaped property on Liansha Resort Island that opened in 2016. The hotel operates on an all-inclusive model, with peak-season rates starting at 2,280 yuan ($340) per person for a two-day, one-night package. Guests receive VIP access to cable cars and unlimited entry to other leisure islands, which offer rides, performances, a pool and evening activities including bonfires, fireworks and stargazing. "The idea is that you can just check in and not worry about anything else," said Li Jin'e, Xiangshawan's marketing director. The leisure islands offer dune buggies, roller coasters and a water world with speedboats and a sandcastle sculpture park that has gone viral on Douyin, China's version of TikTok. Evenings bring candlelight hotpot by the pool and fireworks over the dunes. Li said the resort's philosophy is simple: A vacation means slowing down, even if that means doing nothing at all. "Even lying by the pool for a whole morning — that's a vacation," she said. Yu and her daughter spent their first night stargazing with a guide, who pointed out constellations including the Cowherd and Weaver Girl, stars from a classic Chinese folk tale about lovers separated by the Milky Way. The next day, they explored desert plants and spotted a lizard native to the desert region. International visitors are also increasingly drawn to the desert. Wei Hongyan, general manager of Xiangshawan's marketing company, said the resort offers curated tour routes, foreign-language guides and Halal dining to cater to overseas guests, who come not just for scenery, but to immerse themselves in desert culture. Direct flights from South Korea, Thailand and other regional markets have made access to nearby Ordos Ejin Horo Airport easier. In July, Xiangshawan received about 16,000 foreign tourists — up 176 percent year-on-year — with most coming from South Korea, Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore.

item.title: Former superstar hurdler Liu donates entire salary to charity
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
Former superstar hurdler Liu donates entire salary to charity Olympic champion Liu Xiang said on Thursday that he completed a buyout with Shanghai sports authorities on Sept 1, receiving 494,000 yuan, and would have no further association with the sports bureau. “On Sept 1, I had already completed the buyout and received 494,000 yuan in buyout compensation,” Liu said in a post on his personal social media account. “From now on, I will have no further association with the sports bureau.” The 43-year-old former hurdler also said that he had received a total of 982,935 yuan in salary and subsidies from April 7, 2015, when he retired, until the completion of the buyout. Liu said he donated the entire amount to the China Charity Federation on Sept 2 for disaster relief following mudslides in the Xizang autonomous region. Liu's latest post came after a public dispute over his post-retirement career arrangement triggered widespread discussion on Chinese social media. On Aug 26, Liu posted a photo commemorating his victory at the 2004 Athens Olympics and said the sports authorities had asked him to choose between becoming a coach and accepting a buyout. The Shanghai Sports Bureau said afterward that Liu was an outstanding athlete who had made significant contributions to Shanghai's sports development. It said the Shanghai Competitive Sports Training Management Center had communicated with Liu and would handle his post-retirement arrangement in accordance with relevant national and municipal regulations, mainly through organizational placement or self-employment. In his latest post, Liu also addressed what he described as the issue of being “on the payroll but not at his post”, saying he had not received any formal position or post since his retirement. “I have not received any official post or position since I retired,” Liu said. “I respect the rules and accept that there may have been oversights, but rules should never be an excuse.” He questioned why the issue had taken 11 years to address, saying that the choice between becoming a coach and accepting a buyout had come too late to be regarded as a genuine career choice. Liu said he hoped his case would encourage greater attention to the career transition of retired athletes and called for more flexible and diverse arrangements. “Putting the issue of resettlement in the public eye is not about using public opinion to seek a third option,” he said. “I hope organizations will seriously consider the future of every retired athlete and treat them well.” Liu won the men's 110-meter hurdles at the 2004 Athens Olympics with a time of 12.91 seconds, becoming the first Asian athlete to win an Olympic gold medal in a men's track event. He went on to win the world title in 2007 and set a world record of 12.88 seconds in 2006.

item.title: Hotel robots surprise visitors, streamline operations
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
When Ricky Colomer Goenaga, 32, a designer from Spain, looked around and noticed a delivery robot following him, he wasn't quite sure how to react. New to Shanghai and living at a hotel, he stepped into an elevator — and a white, waist-high box on wheels followed him in. The robot, in Goenaga's words, was rather assertive. It nudged him out of the middle of the elevator, nearly ran over his toes and rattled off something in Chinese he didn't understand. Then it pressed the button for its desired floor and rolled out as soon as the elevator doors opened. "I was like, 'what happened here?'" Goenaga recalled. He said that he wasn't quite sure what the machine even was — bigger and bulkier than, yet nothing like, the robotic vacuums he'd seen. One and a half years on, the sight of a robot gliding through hotel lobbies and corridors no longer fazes him. In March, on a business trip to Beijing, he keyed his room number into the order system and waited. Soon, the robot arrived at his door carrying his packed salad. This time, Goenaga was all grins. He posed for a photograph with the machine and posted it on social media, joking that after being "bullied" by the robot in Shanghai, the two had finally made peace. For many foreign visitors, the robot is among the first surprises they encounter in China. Social media are full of posts about their "meetings" with the machines in their hotels, with comments such as "I'm sharing the elevator with robots!" or "China is on another level of efficiency". In China, however, such robots are no longer a novelty. According to a report released in August by IIM, a Beijing-based industry research organization, the penetration rate of hotel service robots in China exceeded 30 percent in 2025 and is expected to surpass 50 percent by 2030. For hotels, the appeal is simple: Robots can handle repetitive tasks around the clock. "I think they are very useful. They save us plenty of time and improve the efficiency," said Wang Xinyu, a lobby manager at a budget hotel in Beijing. Open since January, the hotel operates three robots across six floors and 372 rooms. Wang said that more than half the guests order takeaway during mealtimes — and that last stretch, from front desk to door, is where the robots step in. When an order lands, the front desk tucks the food into the robot's compartment and punches in the room number. From there, the robot owns it — it hails the elevator, rolls to the door and pings the guest to come grab it. Between rushes, the machines remain parked in corners, charging their batteries. Autoxing Technology Co, the company that makes the robots, was founded in 2020 with ambitions to develop autonomous-driving technology for cars. But the bet proved expensive, prompting the company to narrow its focus. Two years later, it launched its hotel robots. The technology behind them is largely the same, enabling machines to move from one place to another without bumping into any obstacles. "The rapid development of autonomous-driving in China has, to some extent, boosted other robotic applications," said Yang Tianyun, a marketing manager at Autoxing. About 60 percent of Autoxing's business now comes from exports, although differences in regulations across countries can slow deployment. This helps explain why the robots can surprise foreign visitors like Goenaga. "We had never seen anything like that anywhere else in the world," Goenaga said. "I think a lot of people are not aware of how advanced the technology is here." As a designer, Goenaga also likes the robots' cute look. They do not need to look human, he said, adding that a friendly, approachable design is more fitting for hotels, where they interact with families and children.
